study.title: Core training helps pain and function
study.evidence_note: 57 RCTs, 7,705 participants; pain and function improved, but heterogeneity was high.
study.confidence_note: Numbers and design were clear in the full text.
study.impact_line: Core training is reasonable, but the best choice may differ for pain versus function.
summary: 57 RCTs included; 7,705 participants with chronic nonspecific low back pain.
Pain improved versus control in pooled analyses, with Pilates showing the largest pain effect.
Function improved too, with core resistance training looking strongest for ODI.
Quality-of-life mental health effects were small or absent.

pico.p: Adults with chronic nonspecific low back pain
pico.i: Core resistance training, core stability training, or Pilates
pico.c: No exercise, usual care, or non-specific activity
pico.o: Pain, disability, functional status, quality of life

limits: High heterogeneity for pain and ODI.
Included-study mean ages reached 69.57 despite the 18–65 years inclusion criterion.
Publication bias assessment was not reported.
study.bottom_line: Core training improved pain and disability versus control in pooled RCTs for chronic nonspecific low back pain. Pilates and core resistance ranked highest numerically, but subgroup differences were not significant and heterogeneity was high.

methods.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
methods.setting: Four databases to May; adult CNSLBP
methods.intervention: Core resistance training, core stability training, Pilates
methods.comparator: No exercise, standard care, or non-specific activity
methods.follow_up: Mostly short term; many interventions 2-12 weeks

results.detail: 30 studies: pain improved versus control. Pilates had the largest subgroup SMD, but between-subgroup difference was not significant (P=0.24).
29 ODI studies: disability improved versus control. Core resistance had the largest subgroup SMD, but between-subgroup differences were not significant.
Adjusted analysis after removing high-heterogeneity studies remained non-significant.

how_to_apply: Use core training for chronic nonspecific low back pain if exercise is appropriate.
Do not treat Pilates as proven superior for pain; subgroup differences were not significant.
Do not treat core resistance as proven superior for function; subgroup differences were not significant.
Expect short-term gains rather than proven long-term durability.
Use dose suggestions cautiously; meta-regression is observational.
Do not expect meaningful mental-health change from core training alone.
applies_to: Adults with chronic nonspecific low back pain

weaknesses: High heterogeneity in key pooled outcomes.
Many included studies had some concerns or high bias.
Dose-response findings are observational within the review.
funding_conflicts: Funded by Sichuan Provincial Society of Sports Science, Aviation Sports Research Institute, and Central Universities funds.
Authors reported no commercial or financial conflict.

grade.reason: Most included studies were rated some concerns or high risk overall, and blinding was difficult in exercise trials.
Pain and disability analyses showed high heterogeneity before sensitivity analyses.
Population, interventions, comparators, and outcomes match the review question.
CIs are precise for direction but no MCID or smallest worthwhile change is reported.
No publication-bias assessment is reported in the supplied text.

clinical_significance: No MCID or smallest worthwhile change was reported, so clinical size cannot be mapped to a threshold.
Pain and ODI effects were large in SMD terms, but heterogeneity makes exact clinical size uncertain.
The review suggests meaningful short-term benefit, not proof of a single best exercise for all patients.
A useful NNT cannot be derived from the supplied data.
comparator_fairness: Comparators were mixed: no exercise, standard care, or non-specific activity.
Some controls may have been weaker than a true exercise comparator.
Expectation balance was not fully described for all trials.
alternative_explanations: Natural recovery may explain some improvement in short trials.
Regression to the mean could inflate pre-post change.
Contextual effects and supervised attention may contribute.
Co-interventions and uneven control care may have influenced results.
spin: The discussion emphasises modality rankings beyond the non-significant between-group comparisons.
Dose-response recommendations come from meta-regression, not head-to-head dose trials.
The conclusion is stronger than the heterogeneity allows.
fit_with_evidence: Fits prior reviews cited by the authors showing exercise helps chronic low back pain.
Extends earlier work by comparing core resistance, Pilates, and core stability directly.
Still consistent with exercise-first playbook advice for chronic nonspecific low back pain.
external_validity: Likely relevant to an Australian sports-physio caseload for exercise-based low back pain care.
Most studies were short and many participants were younger than typical mixed general practice.
Settings were international and not specifically Australian.
Transfer is best for supervised exercise, not for long-term prognosis claims.
would_change_my_mind: A large head-to-head RCT with low bias and long follow-up showing no difference between modalities.
A review with consistent effects after publication-bias adjustment and lower heterogeneity.
Trials showing durable functional benefit beyond 12 weeks with clear adverse-event reporting.

study.patient_explanation: Exercise-based core training can help chronic low back pain, especially in the short term. Pilates may help pain most, while strength-style core work may help function more, but no one approach suits everyone.
open_questions: Which modality works best long term?
Are benefits maintained after supervision stops?
key_findings: Pain improved versus control in pooled analyses.
Disability improved versus control in pooled analyses.
Pilates and resistance ranked highest numerically; subgroup differences were not significant.
